newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Burundi leader in Tanzania for sanctions summit.
newsitem.headline: Burundi leader in Tanzania for sanctions summit.

text.p: Burundi military leader Major Pierre Buyoya arrived in northern Tanzania on Tuesday for the first regional meeting since neighbours imposed an economic embargo to force him to restore democracy.
Buyoya, accompanied by ministers and officials from his isolated government, went straight into talks with summit host Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa.

Burundian officials said the talks, the first with the Tanzanian leader since Buyoya took power last July, centred on Buyoya's call for a lifting of the embargo imposed after he overthrew Hutu civilian president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya.
"We would like to see the sanctions lifted for sure. The sanctions are hurting the small people," an aide to Buyoya told Reuters.
The summit on Wednesday will decide whether to tighten or lift transport and economic sanctions imposed on July 31 to force Buyoya, a Tutsi, into talks with Hutu rebels.
Wednesday's summit will be attended by heads of state from Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda and Zambia.

The Hutu rebels led by former government minister Leonard Nyangoma took issue with Buyoya's trip to Tanzania, saying he had not met conditions laid out by neighbouring heads of state for sanctions to be lifted.
"When you (presidents) decided against the Burundi military junta, you gave a series of conditions to be met by the junta before contemplating to lift them," said a statement signed by Nyangoma.
"Today Buyoya is trying to mislead people by pretending that he met the conditions, while this is untrue," Nyangoma added.
Nyangoma's Hutu guerrilla army is waging a ruthless war against Buyoya's Tutsi-dominated army for a greater political stake in the ethnically-torn tiny central African nation.
A United Nations study of the sanctions released this week found no hard evidence they had succeeded in their political aims while smuggling was weakening their impact.
Initial findings issued on Tuesday by the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs suggested Burundi sanctions should be retargeted to protect the vulnerable and more items exempted for aid agencies.

"While it is possible that concessions by the regime may, in part, be the result of prolonged sanctions, there is no concrete evidence that sanctions have been (politically) successful," said researchers from Brown University in the United States.
The report was released by DHA in Nairobi on the eve of the Arusha summit.

The seizure of east Zaire since October by Tutsi-dominated rebels has benefited Buyoya's junta because Hutu rebels based in Zaire were uprooted. Kinshasa has accused Burundi of sending its troops into Zaire to aid the rebellion.

Burundi's government denies such accusations, as does Rwanda and Uganda. Kenya, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zaire and Zambia said when they imposed sanctions that they expected them to achieve their main objectives within one to two months.
